title: DNS Security (DNSSEC) Hashed Authenticated Denial of Existence
summary: Adds the NSEC3 record to DNSSEC as an alternative way to prove that a name does not exist. Unlike NSEC, it uses hashed names to make it harder to list every name in a zone, and it supports opt-out for zones with many delegations. It is a standards-track specification. Later RFCs update it.

eli5.summary: When you ask a librarian for a book that does not exist, they must prove it. NSEC3 proves it with a scrambled list, so nobody can read all the real titles.

questions: how does dnssec prove a name does not exist
how to prevent dnssec zone enumeration
how does nsec3 prevent zone walking
what is the nsec3 opt-out flag
subtitle: A DNSSEC record that proves a name does not exist without handing out a list of every name in the zone.

tldr.problem: The NSEC record proves that a DNS name does not exist by listing neighbouring names, so anyone can walk the chain and enumerate the whole zone. Securing delegations to unsigned zones can also be very costly for large, delegation-centric zones.
tldr.mechanism: NSEC3 orders hashed owner names instead of the real names, using a salt and a number of hash iterations. An Opt-Out flag lets unsigned delegations be left out of the chain.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 6840, RFC 6944, RFC 9077, RFC 9157, RFC 9276 and RFC 9905. Hashing makes enumeration more expensive but does not remove it.

today: RFC 5155 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 6840, RFC 6944, RFC 9077, RFC 9157, RFC 9276 and RFC 9905, so read it together with those updates.

sections.title: The Problem with NSEC
sections.content:
DNSSEC needs a way to prove that a name does not exist. The NSEC record does this by listing two canonically ordered names and showing that nothing exists between them. The side effect is that the full set of NSEC records lists every name in the zone, so a zone can be enumerated trivially by querying for names that do not exist.

The RFC points out why this matters. An enumerated zone can be a source of probable e-mail addresses for spam, or a key for many WHOIS queries that reveal registrant data a registry may be legally obliged to protect. Registries that prohibit copying of their zone data find that NSEC makes the policy unenforceable.

A second problem is cost. Securing delegations to unsigned zones is expensive relative to the benefit for large, delegation-centric zones and for zones where insecure delegations change rapidly. NSEC3 is offered as an alternative that addresses both issues.
sections.eli5: A plain list of "nothing between here and here" lets a nosy person read every name by following the list. NSEC3 hides the names so the list stops giving them away.

sections.title: The NSEC3 and NSEC3PARAM Records
sections.content:
The NSEC3 record (type 50) lists the record types present at one original owner name and gives the next hashed owner name in hash order. The complete set forms a chain of hashed names around the zone, and the last record points back to the first. The owner name of each NSEC3 record is the base32 encoding of the hash, prepended as a single label to the zone name.

Its data has these fields: Hash Algorithm, Flags (only the Opt-Out flag, the least significant bit, is defined), Iterations, Salt Length and Salt, Hash Length, Next Hashed Owner Name (raw binary, not base32, and without the zone name), and Type Bit Maps (encoded as in NSEC). The record SHOULD have the same TTL as the SOA minimum field.

The NSEC3PARAM record (type 51) sits at the zone apex and repeats the first four fields so authoritative servers know which parameters to use. It is not used by validators or resolvers. Its Opt-Out flag is not used, and NSEC3PARAM records with nonzero flags MUST be ignored. If there are several NSEC3PARAM records, there are several valid chains, and the server picks one.
sections.eli5: Each entry in the scrambled list says what kinds of things exist at one scrambled name and where the next scrambled name is. A separate note at the top of the zone tells the server how the scrambling was done.

sections.title: Calculating the Hash
sections.content:
The hash uses the Hash Algorithm, the Salt and the Iterations fields. The hash is applied to the owner name together with the salt, then the result is hashed again with the salt appended, once for each iteration; the exact definition is in the box below.

The owner name is first put in canonical form: fully expanded with no name compression and fully qualified, with uppercase US-ASCII letters changed to lowercase. A wildcard name is hashed in its original unexpanded form, including the asterisk label. The only hash algorithm defined is 1, SHA-1.

The salt is appended before hashing so that one precomputed dictionary cannot be used against every zone, and the iterations make each guess more costly for an attacker.
sections.eli5: To scramble a name, you mix it with a secret-looking ingredient and put it through the blender, then run the result through the blender again several times.

sections.title: Opt-Out for Unsigned Delegations
sections.content:
Normally the security status of a child zone is proven by the presence or absence of a DS record, backed by a signed NSEC3 record at the hashed name of the delegation. With the Opt-Out flag set, insecure delegations may exist in the signed zone without an NSEC3 record of their own. This is what lets very large zones with mostly unsigned delegations add and remove those delegations without recalculating and re-signing the chain.

An Opt-Out NSEC3 record does not claim that the delegations it covers exist or do not exist. It still asserts the existence or non-existence of other authoritative data. A zone may mix Opt-Out and ordinary NSEC3 records. An ordinary one MUST NOT have insecure delegations in its span, and an Opt-Out one MUST cover only hashed names of insecure delegations.

The RFC strongly RECOMMENDS using Opt-Out sparingly. Zone signing tools SHOULD NOT default to it and MAY choose not to support it at all, because the existence of an insecure delegation in an Opt-Out span cannot be proven.
sections.eli5: Opt-Out is like saying, "For this stretch of the list I won't promise whether certain unlocked doors exist." It saves work but gives up some certainty.

sections.title: Proving a Name Does Not Exist
sections.content:
Servers replace the NSEC records of ordinary DNSSEC negative responses with NSEC3 records that prove the same facts. Most proofs rely on a closest encloser, the longest existing ancestor of the queried name. A closest encloser proof has up to two NSEC3 records. One matches the closest encloser, which shows it exists. The other covers the "next closer" name, the name one label longer, which shows that the queried name and any ancestors below the encloser do not exist.

For a name error (the name does not exist), the response MUST also include an NSEC3 record covering the wildcard at the closest encloser, so up to three NSEC3 records are returned. For a no data response, the NSEC3 record that matches the name MUST NOT have the bit for the query type or for CNAME set. Wildcard answers and referrals to unsigned subzones have their own rules, and in Opt-Out zones the proof uses the closest provable encloser.

Validators check the same proofs. They MUST ignore NSEC3 records with unknown hash algorithms, and they MUST NOT have the AD bit set on responses whose proof depends on an Opt-Out record covering the next closer name, because not all of the data was cryptographically verified. If the hash of a missing name collides with an existing NSEC3 owner name, the server MUST return RCODE 2 (server failure).
sections.eli5: To show a book isn't on the shelf, the librarian shows the nearest real shelf label and a gap in the scrambled list where the book would have to be.

sections.title: Limits on Iterations
sections.content:
More iterations make dictionary attacks more expensive, but also cost the server and every validator more work. The RFC therefore sets an upper limit based on the size of the smallest zone signing key. A zone owner MUST NOT use a higher value than the table allows, and a resolver MAY treat a response with a higher value as insecure after checking the signature over the NSEC3 record.

The values come from the approximate ratio between the cost of an SHA-1 calculation and an RSA verification. The same table MUST be used regardless of the key algorithm.

The hashed name also has to fit in a domain name. With SHA-1 the hash is 160 bits, which becomes 32 base32 characters. With the label length octet that is 33 octets, so the zone name can be at most 222 octets long (255 minus 33).
sections.eli5: The more times you blend, the harder it is for a snoop, but the more work for everybody who checks. So there is a limit that depends on how strong the lock is.

sections.title: Compatibility and Transition
sections.content:
NSEC3 is not generally backwards compatible with RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035, and resolvers that do not know it may fail to validate its responses. To avoid that, the RFC allocates two new DNSKEY algorithm identifiers: 6, DSA-NSEC3-SHA1 (an alias for algorithm 3) and 7, RSASHA1-NSEC3-SHA1 (an alias for algorithm 5). Zones signed with NSEC3 MUST use only these identifiers. Resolvers that do not recognise them treat the zone as insecure instead of failing.

Moving a signed zone from NSEC to NSEC3 has four steps: switch the DNSKEYs to the alias algorithms, add signed NSEC3 records (with the NSEC3PARAM RRset added last), let the server switch to NSEC3 responses, then remove the NSEC records. Going back reverses the steps. The RFC defines no mechanism for moving between NSEC3 hash algorithms.
sections.eli5: Old readers can't understand the scrambled list, so the zone puts on a label they don't recognise and they politely skip checking it, instead of getting confused.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
NSEC3 does not stop dictionary attacks. An attacker can collect all NSEC3 records and hash likely names to compare. This is substantially more expensive than reading NSEC records, and its cost can be tuned with the number of iterations. A precomputed dictionary is defeated by changing the salt regularly, and the salt SHOULD be at least 64 bits long and unpredictable.

High iteration values bring two risks. Because validators may treat such responses as insecure, an attacker holding one signed NSEC3 record with a high value can replace the real ones in a response and downgrade it. High values also give an attacker a denial-of-service opportunity against servers, which must compute several hashes per negative or wildcard response.

Walking the NSEC3 records still reveals how many records the zone has and which types exist. Hash collisions are possible in principle but, with SHA-1, are on the order of 1 in 2^160.
sections.eli5: A very determined snoop can still guess names and check them against the scrambled list. Changing the secret ingredient often and blending more times make the guessing slower and harder.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Only the Opt-Out bit, the least significant, is defined.

fields.name: Iterations
fields.desc: Additional times the hash is applied.

data.title: NSEC3 hash definition
data.code:
IH(salt, x, 0) = H(x || salt), and
IH(salt, x, k) = H(IH(salt, x, k-1) || salt), if k > 0

hash of owner name = IH(salt, owner name, iterations)
